newsitem.title: USA: N. Calif. grand jury probes Raiders stadium deal.
newsitem.headline: N. Calif. grand jury probes Raiders stadium deal.

text.p: An Alameda County, Calif., grand jury has recently heard testimony from officials involved in a $200 million Raiders football stadium deal, according to some of those who testified before the panel.

One of those who testified, George Vukasin, president of the Oakland-Alameda County Coliseum board, said he spoke to the county grand jury in mid-September about the controversial stadium transactions.
Another person who testified confirmed that the grand jury was looking into the stadium deal.
Assistant Alameda County District Attorney Stacy Walthall, who advises the grand jury, would not comment on whether the panel was reviewing the Raiders deal.
"We're not allowed to talk about who testified or what anyone might have said about any ongoing investigation, Walthall said.

Walthall added, however, that the grand jury was "interested in the fiscal affairs of the county, and this (Raiders) issue certainly would have an impact on the fiscal affairs of the city (of Oakland) and the county."
For months, the coliseum deal that brought the Raiders football team back to Oakland has been marred by financial and operational problems, drawing fire from public officials.
Officials warn that Oakland and Alameda County could be forced to dip into their general funds to cover unanticipated costs associated with improvements at the coliseum.

In September 1995, the Oakland-Alameda County Coliseum Authority sold nearly $200 million of taxable bonds to pay for renovations to the coliseum. Annual payments on the coliseum bonds are about $14.3 million.

The money to pay investors was supposed to come primarily from the sale of at least 45,000 personal seat licenses, which give fans the right to purchase season tickets. But officials say sales of seat licenses have lagged far behind projections.
"The grand jury has a responsibility" to look into these matters, Vukasin said. "There have been a lot of problems with the ticket plans. So they're looking at it."
Vukasin said the grand jury appeared to be focusing on how the deal was structured. "It was a confidential session and I intend to honor that," he said, declining further comment.
